## Species observed in Germany and common name lookup

To make charts easier to read, English common names are shown next to Latin names wherever possible. As described in the Methodology section, the GlobalGeoTree dataset contains `species_key`, a unique GBIF identifier for each species. This key is used to query the GBIF vernacular-names API once and cache the result in `data/external/species_common_names.csv`. On every subsequent render, the report reads from that file.

```{r germany-species-count}
german_species_for_names <- germany |>
  filter(!is.na(level3_species), level3_species != "") |>
  group_by(level3_species, species_key) |>
  summarise(de_observations = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(de_observations))

species_count_summary <- tibble::tibble(
  metric = c("Unique species in German observations", "Species with a valid GBIF species key"),
  value = c(
    format_number(n_distinct(german_species_for_names$level3_species)),
    format_number(sum(!is.na(german_species_for_names$species_key) &
                        german_species_for_names$species_key != ""))
  )
)
nice_table(species_count_summary, "German species overview")
```

```{r fetch-species-names}
species_names_path <- "data/external/species_common_names.csv"

if (!file.exists(species_names_path)) {
  if (!requireNamespace("jsonlite", quietly = TRUE)) {
    stop("Install jsonlite to fetch species names: install.packages('jsonlite')")
  }

  species_with_key <- german_species_for_names |>
    filter(!is.na(species_key), species_key != "")

  # Fetches the first English common name for a species from the GBIF API.
  # A small delay (0.08s) is added between requests to avoid overloading the API.
  fetch_en_name <- function(key) {
    url <- paste0("https://api.gbif.org/v1/species/", key, "/vernacularNames?limit=30")
    resp <- tryCatch(jsonlite::fromJSON(url, simplifyDataFrame = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)
    Sys.sleep(0.08)
    if (is.null(resp) || !is.data.frame(resp$results) || nrow(resp$results) == 0) return(NA_character_)
    en <- resp$results$vernacularName[resp$results$language == "eng"]
    if (length(en) == 0) return(NA_character_)
    en[1]
  }

  species_with_key$common_name_en <- vapply(species_with_key$species_key, fetch_en_name, character(1))
  write.csv(species_with_key, species_names_path, row.names = FALSE)
}

species_names_raw <- read.csv(species_names_path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE) |> tibble::as_tibble()
species_common_names <- species_names_raw |>
  select(level3_species, common_name_en) |>
  filter(!is.na(common_name_en), common_name_en != "")

fetch_names_status <- tibble::tibble(
  metric = c("Species queried from GBIF", "Species with an English common name"),
  value = c(format_number(nrow(species_names_raw)), format_number(nrow(species_common_names)))
)
nice_table(fetch_names_status, "GBIF common names lookup result")
```

Species without an English name in GBIF are shown with their Latin name only in charts. The cached file can be deleted and re-generated at any time by deleting `data/external/species_common_names.csv` and re-rendering the report.

# Germany: National Patterns

This section examines how tree observations are distributed across Germany as a whole, addressing RQ4.1 through RQ4.4: spatial concentration, temporal trends, source structure, and Bundesland-level variation.

## Load Bundesländer boundaries

Bundesländer polygons are needed to draw state boundaries on Germany maps and to assign observations to federal states. The code first looks for a local GeoJSON file; if it is not found, the public GISCO NUTS1 file is downloaded.

```{r load-bundeslaender}
bundeslaender_result <- read_geojson_local_or_url(
  bundeslaender_local_path, gisco_nuts1_url, "Bundesländer / NUTS1"
)
bundeslaender <- bundeslaender_result$data

if (!is.null(bundeslaender)) {
  if ("cntr_code" %in% names(bundeslaender)) {
    bundeslaender <- bundeslaender |> filter(as.character(cntr_code) == "DE")
  }
  if ("levl_code" %in% names(bundeslaender)) {
    bundeslaender <- bundeslaender |> filter(as.character(levl_code) == "1")
  }
  name_col <- intersect(c("name_latn", "nuts_name", "name", "nuts_id"), names(bundeslaender))[1]
  if (is.na(name_col)) {
    bundeslaender$bundesland <- paste("Bundesland", seq_len(nrow(bundeslaender)))
  } else {
    bundeslaender$bundesland <- as.character(bundeslaender[[name_col]])
  }
  bundeslaender <- bundeslaender |>
    select(bundesland, geometry) |>
    filter(!is.na(bundesland), bundesland != "")
}

has_bundeslaender <- !is.null(bundeslaender) && nrow(bundeslaender) > 0

bundeslaender_status <- tibble::tibble(
  item = c("Boundary status", "Number of Bundesländer polygons"),
  value = c(bundeslaender_result$note, ifelse(has_bundeslaender, format_number(nrow(bundeslaender)), "0"))
)
nice_table(bundeslaender_status, "Bundesländer boundary check")
```

```{r load-nuts3}
nuts3_result <- read_geojson_local_or_url(nuts3_local_path, gisco_nuts3_url, "NUTS3")
nuts3 <- nuts3_result$data
```

## Distribution of observations in Germany

This section addresses **RQ4.1**: where are observations spatially concentrated across Germany? As described in the Methodology section, three density visualisation styles are shown to ensure that the choice of map type does not hide any spatial features. The primary map uses smooth filled density contours; two alternative views show the same data with different visual treatments.

```{r germany-distribution-main, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=7}
germany_points_for_maps <- sample_up_to(germany, 70000)
germany_boundary_for_maps <- if (has_bundeslaender) dplyr::bind_rows(bundeslaender) else NULL

if (nrow(germany_points_for_maps) < 3) {
  empty_plot("Not enough Germany observations were available for the distribution maps.")
} else if (germany_distribution_map_type == "smooth_fill") {
  plot_filled_density_map(
    points_data = germany_points_for_maps,
    boundary_data = germany_boundary_for_maps,
    title = "Germany observations: smooth filled density",
    subtitle = "A cleaner hotspot view that is easy to read in a report.",
    caption = "This shows recording density in the dataset, not true tree abundance.",
    xlim = germany_xlim, ylim = germany_ylim, bins = 10, alpha = 0.90
  )
} else {
  plot_points_only_map(
    points_data = germany_points_for_maps,
    boundary_data = germany_boundary_for_maps,
    title = "Germany observations: sampled points",
    subtitle = "A simple raw-point reference map.",
    caption = paste("Displayed points:", format_number(nrow(germany_points_for_maps)), "of", format_number(nrow(germany)), "Germany observations."),
    xlim = germany_xlim, ylim = germany_ylim, point_alpha = 0.10, point_size = 0.22
  )
}
```

**Interpretation.** Darker areas show where more observations were recorded. These hotspots should be read as observation intensity rather than tree abundance: a location can appear dense because observers are active there, because a platform has strong coverage, or simply because access is easier.

### Alternative view: points with density contours

This variant overlays individual observation points with density contour lines. It preserves the ability to see individual records while still showing the broader concentration zones that the filled density map highlights.

```{r germany-distribution-contours, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=7}
if (nrow(germany_points_for_maps) < 3) {
  empty_plot("Not enough Germany observations were available for the comparison maps.")
} else {
  plot_points_contours_map(
    points_data = germany_points_for_maps,
    boundary_data = germany_boundary_for_maps,
    title = "Germany observations: points plus density contours",
    subtitle = "Individual sampled records are visible alongside the broader concentration zones.",
    caption = paste("Displayed points:", format_number(nrow(germany_points_for_maps)), "of", format_number(nrow(germany)), "Germany observations."),
    xlim = germany_xlim, ylim = germany_ylim, point_alpha = 0.10, point_size = 0.22, bins = 10
  )
}
```

### Alternative view: raw observation points

This variant shows only the sampled points with no smoothing at all. It gives the most direct view of where individual records are located, though it can be harder to identify concentration zones at this resolution.

```{r germany-distribution-points, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=7}
if (nrow(germany_points_for_maps) < 1) {
  empty_plot("No Germany observations were available for the point map.")
} else {
  plot_points_only_map(
    points_data = germany_points_for_maps,
    boundary_data = germany_boundary_for_maps,
    title = "Germany observations: sampled points",
    subtitle = "Raw-point reference map with no smoothing.",
    caption = paste("Displayed points:", format_number(nrow(germany_points_for_maps)), "of", format_number(nrow(germany)), "Germany observations."),
    xlim = germany_xlim, ylim = germany_ylim, point_alpha = 0.10, point_size = 0.22
  )
}
```

## Observations by year

This chart addresses **RQ4.2**: how has recording activity changed over time in Germany? A dataset dominated by a few recent years may show spatial patterns that reflect current platform growth rather than long-term tree distribution.

```{r de-observations-by-year, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.8}
year_counts <- germany |>
  filter(!is.na(year), year >= 1900, year <= as.integer(format(Sys.Date(), "%Y"))) |>
  count(year, name = "observations") |>
  arrange(year)

if (nrow(year_counts) == 0) {
  empty_plot("No usable year values were found in the Germany rows.")
} else {
  ggplot(year_counts, aes(x = year, y = observations)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.75, fill = "steelblue") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.6, color = "gray25") +
    geom_point(size = 1.8, color = "gray25") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::pretty_breaks()) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format()) +
    labs(
      title = "Germany observations by year",
      subtitle = "Annual counts show when the Germany subset was most strongly represented.",
      x = "Year", y = "Observations"
    ) +
    theme_gtree()
}
```

**Interpretation.** Peaks in this chart reflect peaks in recording activity, not necessarily more trees. A strong upward trend in recent years is common in citizen-science datasets as more users join the platforms.

## Observations by source on the country map

The year distribution above shows *when* Germany observations were recorded. The next question is *who* recorded them — which platforms contribute the most records, and do they cover the country differently? This section addresses **RQ4.3**: do different data sources show different spatial footprints? Each panel shows where one source group collected its records.

```{r de-source-groups}
source_counts_de <- germany |>
  count(source_raw, name = "observations", sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(share = observations / sum(observations), source_short = make_source_label(source_raw))

top_sources_de <- source_counts_de |> slice_head(n = 5) |> pull(source_raw)

germany_sources <- germany |>
  mutate(
    source_display = if_else(source_raw %in% top_sources_de, make_source_label(source_raw), "Other sources"),
    source_display = stringr::str_wrap(source_display, width = 20)
  )

# Counts for the bar chart
de_source_counts <- germany_sources |>
  count(source_display, name = "observations", sort = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    share = observations / sum(observations),
    label = paste0(format_number(observations), " (", format_percent(share), ")"),
    source_display = factor(source_display, levels = rev(source_display))
  )

source_map_data_de <- germany_sources |>
  group_by(source_display) |>
  group_modify(~ sample_up_to(.x, max_points_per_source_group)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(source_display = factor(source_display, levels = levels(de_source_counts$source_display)))
```

```{r de-source-map, fig.width=10, fig.height=7}
p <- ggplot()
if (has_bundeslaender) {
  p <- p + geom_sf(data = bundeslaender, fill = "gray97", color = "gray70", linewidth = 0.2)
}
p +
  geom_point(data = source_map_data_de, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = source_display),
             alpha = 0.20, size = 0.45) +
  facet_wrap(~ source_display, ncol = 3) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2", guide = "none") +
  coord_sf(xlim = germany_xlim, ylim = germany_ylim, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Spatial footprint of major observation sources in Germany",
    subtitle = "Each panel shows sampled observation points from one source group.",
    caption = paste("Maximum displayed points per source group:", format_number(max_points_per_source_group))
  ) +
  theme_map_gtree()
```

**Interpretation.** If source panels look visually different, this is evidence of source bias: the national density map then reflects a mix of ecological signal and platform coverage.

## Observations by source (bar chart)

The map above shows *where* each source records; this bar chart shows *how many* records each source contributes.

```{r de-source-bar-chart, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=5}
ggplot(de_source_counts, aes(x = source_display, y = observations)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.05, size = 3) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.20))) +
  labs(
    title = "Germany observations by source group",
    subtitle = "The same grouping is used in the country map above.",
    x = NULL, y = "Observations"
  ) +
  theme_gtree()
```

**Interpretation.** The largest bar identifies the dominant source. A single dominant source can strongly shape the density patterns seen on all subsequent maps.

::: {.callout-note}
**Two Pl@ntNet source names.** `Pl@ntNet observations` and `Pl@ntNet auto ID` are both Pl@ntNet-derived but represent different validation routes: one is the regular shared-observation dataset, and the other contains automatically identified occurrences. They are therefore kept separate throughout this report.
:::

## Observations mapped to Bundesländer

Having seen the sources, we now look at where their records land across Germany's sixteen federal states. To answer **RQ4.4**, observations are assigned to Bundesländer using a spatial join — each observation's coordinates are matched to the boundary polygon it falls within.

```{r bundesland-spatial-join}
if (has_bundeslaender) {
  # Spatial join: assign each observation to the Bundesland whose polygon contains it
  germany_bundeslaender <- sf::st_join(germany_points, bundeslaender, left = FALSE, join = sf::st_within) |>
    sf::st_drop_geometry() |> tibble::as_tibble()

  # Aggregate: count observations, species, and sources per Bundesland
  bundesland_counts <- germany_bundeslaender |>
    group_by(bundesland) |>
    summarise(observations = n(), species = n_distinct(level3_species),
              sources = n_distinct(source_raw), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(observations))

  # Join counts back to the boundary polygons for the choropleth map
  bundesland_map <- bundeslaender |>
    left_join(bundesland_counts, by = "bundesland") |>
    mutate(observations = dplyr::coalesce(observations, 0L),
           species = dplyr::coalesce(species, 0L),
           sources = dplyr::coalesce(sources, 0L))
} else {
  germany_bundeslaender <- tibble::tibble()
  bundesland_counts <- tibble::tibble()
  bundesland_map <- NULL
}

bundesland_join_check <- tibble::tibble(
  metric = c("Germany observations before join", "Matched to a Bundesland", "Bundesländer with observations"),
  value = c(format_number(nrow(germany)), format_number(nrow(germany_bundeslaender)), format_number(nrow(bundesland_counts)))
)
nice_table(bundesland_join_check, "Bundesland spatial join check")
```

```{r bundesland-bar-chart, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=6}
if (nrow(bundesland_counts) == 0) {
  empty_plot("Bundesländer counts are unavailable because the boundary file was not loaded.")
} else {
  ggplot(bundesland_counts, aes(x = reorder(bundesland, observations), y = observations)) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    geom_text(aes(label = format_number(observations)), hjust = -0.05, size = 3) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
    labs(
      title = "Germany observations by Bundesland",
      subtitle = "Observation counts are based on spatially joining coordinates to GISCO NUTS1 boundaries.",
      x = NULL, y = "Observations"
    ) +
    theme_gtree()
}
```

```{r bundesland-map, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
if (is.null(bundesland_map)) {
  empty_plot("Bundesländer map is unavailable because the boundary file was not loaded.")
} else {
  ggplot(bundesland_map) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = observations), color = "white", linewidth = 0.35) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", trans = "sqrt", labels = scales::comma_format()) +
    labs(
      title = "Observation frequency by Bundesland",
      subtitle = "Darker Bundesländer contain more Germany observations in the dataset.",
      fill = "Observations",
      caption = "Boundaries: GISCO NUTS1 regions. Counts: GlobalGeoTree Germany subset."
    ) +
    theme_map_gtree()
}
```

**Interpretation.** Together, the bar chart provides exact rankings while the map shows whether high-record states cluster in one part of Germany. Differences between Bundesländer reflect population density, platform coverage, and observer activity rather than differences in actual tree abundance.

# Berlin

Berlin is the first of three focal regions examined in detail. As a city-state, Berlin's entire area is urban, which may produce recording patterns quite different from larger, more rural federal states. This is also our team's home city, giving us local context for interpreting the results.

## Load Berlin district boundaries

Berlin is handled separately because a finer boundary layer than Bundesländer is needed for city-level analysis. The district boundaries come from an open-data project and provide polygons for Berlin's local areas (Ortsteile).

```{r load-berlin-boundaries}
berlin_result <- read_geojson_local_or_url(berlin_local_path, berlin_district_url, "Berlin district/local-area")
berlin_districts <- berlin_result$data

if (!is.null(berlin_districts)) {
  name_col <- intersect(c("name", "bezirk", "district", "gemeinde_name", "gen", "ortsteil"), names(berlin_districts))[1]
  if (is.na(name_col)) {
    berlin_districts$district <- paste("Area", seq_len(nrow(berlin_districts)))
  } else {
    berlin_districts$district <- as.character(berlin_districts[[name_col]])
  }
  berlin_districts <- berlin_districts |>
    select(district, geometry) |>
    filter(!is.na(district), district != "")
}

has_berlin_districts <- !is.null(berlin_districts) && nrow(berlin_districts) > 0

berlin_boundary_status <- tibble::tibble(
  item = c("Berlin boundary status", "Number of Berlin polygons"),
  value = c(berlin_result$note, ifelse(has_berlin_districts, format_number(nrow(berlin_districts)), "0"))
)
nice_table(berlin_boundary_status, "Berlin boundary check")
```

## Berlin observations

```{r berlin-filter-and-summary}
if (has_berlin_districts) {
  district_bbox <- sf::st_bbox(berlin_districts)
  germany_points_near_berlin <- germany_points |>
    filter(longitude >= district_bbox[["xmin"]], longitude <= district_bbox[["xmax"]],
           latitude >= district_bbox[["ymin"]], latitude <= district_bbox[["ymax"]])
  berlin_joined <- sf::st_join(germany_points_near_berlin, berlin_districts, left = FALSE, join = sf::st_within)
  berlin <- berlin_joined |> sf::st_drop_geometry() |> tibble::as_tibble()
  berlin_filter_method <- "Spatial join to Berlin district/local-area polygons"
} else {
  berlin <- germany |>
    filter(longitude >= berlin_bbox$lon_min, longitude <= berlin_bbox$lon_max,
           latitude >= berlin_bbox$lat_min, latitude <= berlin_bbox$lat_max) |>
    mutate(district = NA_character_)
  berlin_filter_method <- "Approximate Berlin bounding box fallback"
}

berlin_summary <- make_state_summary(berlin, "Berlin", berlin_filter_method)
nice_table(berlin_summary, "Berlin observation summary")
```

## Berlin observation sources

Source composition is important context for every Berlin map. If one platform dominates, Berlin hotspots may partly reflect that platform's recording behaviour rather than tree distribution.

```{r berlin-source-summary}
berlin_source_counts <- make_source_counts(berlin)

berlin_source_counts |>
  mutate(observations = format_number(observations), share = format_percent(share)) |>
  nice_table("Berlin observations by source")
```

```{r berlin-source-bar, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=5}
ggplot(berlin_source_counts, aes(x = source_short, y = observations)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.05, size = 3) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
  labs(title = "Berlin observations by source", x = NULL, y = "Observations") +
  theme_gtree()
```

## Spatial distribution of Berlin observations

This map addresses **RQ4.5** for Berlin: which parts of the city show the highest recording density? Because Berlin is geographically compact, a single density map with overlaid district boundaries is sufficient to show spatial patterns.

```{r berlin-spatial-distribution, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
berlin_points_for_map <- sample_up_to(berlin, max_berlin_points)

if (nrow(berlin_points_for_map) < 3) {
  empty_plot("Not enough Berlin observations were available for a density map.")
} else if (has_berlin_districts) {
  ggplot() +
    stat_density_2d_filled(data = berlin_points_for_map,
                           aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, fill = after_stat(level)),
                           contour_var = "ndensity", bins = 8, alpha = 0.78) +
    geom_sf(data = berlin_districts, fill = NA, color = "gray25", linewidth = 0.35) +
    geom_point(data = berlin_points_for_map, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude), alpha = 0.14, size = 0.35) +
    coord_sf() +
    scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "C", direction = -1, name = "Density") +
    labs(title = "Tree observation density in Berlin",
         subtitle = "Filled contours show observation density; local-area borders provide spatial context.",
         x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_map_gtree()
} else {
  ggplot(berlin_points_for_map, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude)) +
    stat_density_2d_filled(contour_var = "ndensity", bins = 8, alpha = 0.8) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.12, size = 0.35) +
    coord_fixed() +
    scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "C", direction = -1, name = "Density") +
    labs(title = "Tree observation density in Berlin",
         subtitle = "District borders were unavailable, so this map uses the Berlin bounding-box fallback.",
         x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") +
    theme_gtree()
}
```

**Interpretation.** The density map highlights which parts of Berlin have the most recorded tree observations. High-density areas are likely to correspond to parks, green corridors, and neighbourhoods with active observers rather than necessarily having more trees than other areas.

## Berlin local areas: observations and species

```{r berlin-district-summary}
if ("district" %in% names(berlin) && any(!is.na(berlin$district))) {
  berlin_district_counts <- berlin |>
    filter(!is.na(district), district != "") |>
    group_by(district) |>
    summarise(observations = n(), species = n_distinct(level3_species),
              sources = n_distinct(source_raw), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(observations))
} else {
  berlin_district_counts <- tibble::tibble()
}

if (nrow(berlin_district_counts) > 0) {
  berlin_district_counts |>
    slice_head(n = 20) |>
    mutate(observations = format_number(observations), species = format_number(species), sources = format_number(sources)) |>
    nice_table("Top Berlin local areas by observation count")
} else {
  nice_table(tibble::tibble(note = "Berlin local-area counts are unavailable because polygons were not loaded."))
}
```

```{r berlin-district-bar, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=6}
if (nrow(berlin_district_counts) == 0) {
  empty_plot("Berlin local-area counts are unavailable because polygons were not loaded.")
} else {
  berlin_district_counts |>
    slice_head(n = 20) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = reorder(district, observations), y = observations)) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    geom_text(aes(label = format_number(observations)), hjust = -0.05, size = 3) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
    labs(title = "Berlin observations by local area", subtitle = "Only the top 20 areas are shown.", x = NULL, y = "Observations") +
    theme_gtree()
}
```

```{r berlin-species-bar, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=6}
if (nrow(berlin_district_counts) == 0) {
  empty_plot("Berlin local-area species counts are unavailable because polygons were not loaded.")
} else {
  berlin_district_counts |>
    arrange(desc(species)) |>
    slice_head(n = 20) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = reorder(district, species), y = species)) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    geom_text(aes(label = format_number(species)), hjust = -0.05, size = 3) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
    labs(title = "Recorded species by Berlin local area", x = NULL, y = "Recorded species") +
    theme_gtree()
}
```

```{r berlin-district-map, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
if (has_berlin_districts && nrow(berlin_district_counts) > 0) {
  berlin_district_map <- berlin_districts |>
    left_join(berlin_district_counts, by = "district") |>
    mutate(observations = dplyr::coalesce(observations, 0L))
  ggplot(berlin_district_map) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = observations), color = "white", linewidth = 0.25) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", trans = "sqrt", labels = scales::comma_format()) +
    labs(title = "Observation frequency by Berlin local area",
         subtitle = "Square-root scaling keeps both high and medium-count areas visible.",
         fill = "Observations") +
    theme_map_gtree()
} else {
  empty_plot("Berlin local-area map is unavailable because polygons were not loaded.")
}
```

**Interpretation.** The bar charts rank local areas by observation count and species count separately, while the choropleth map shows the spatial pattern. Local areas with both high observation counts and high species richness may genuinely be more biodiverse or may simply have more active recording communities.

## Top recorded species in Berlin

```{r berlin-top-species}
berlin_named <- add_species_display_name(berlin)

berlin_top_species <- berlin_named |>
  count(level3_species, species_display_name, display_common_name_en, sort = TRUE, name = "observations") |>
  mutate(share = observations / sum(observations))

berlin_top_species |>
  slice_head(n = 15) |>
  select(scientific_name = level3_species, common_name_en = display_common_name_en, observations, share) |>
  mutate(observations = format_number(observations), share = format_percent(share)) |>
  nice_table("Top recorded species in Berlin")
```

```{r berlin-top-species-bar, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=6}
berlin_top_species |>
  slice_head(n = 15) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(species_display_name, observations), y = observations)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = format_number(observations)), hjust = -0.05, size = 3) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(title = "Most recorded tree species in Berlin",
       subtitle = "English common names are shown where available; counts show records, not true abundance.",
       x = NULL, y = "Observations") +
  theme_gtree()
```

**Interpretation.** The most frequently recorded species in Berlin reflect the city's urban tree stock, which includes both native species and commonly planted street and park trees. High observation counts for a species can indicate that it is genuinely common, that it is easy to identify and therefore often recorded by citizen-science users, or both.

## Berlin oak tree groups

This section addresses **RQ4.8** and extends the analysis beyond the standard research questions to demonstrate a practical application of the dataset. Oak trees are a public-health concern in Berlin because the oak processionary moth (*Thaumetopoea processionea*) can cause allergic reactions and skin irritation in people and pets near affected trees. Mapping recorded oak locations can help identify areas where monitoring or public warnings may be needed.

```{r berlin-oak-summary}
berlin_oaks <- berlin |>
  filter(
    stringr::str_to_lower(as.character(level2_genus)) == "quercus" |
      stringr::str_detect(stringr::str_to_lower(as.character(level3_species)), "^quercus\\b")
  )

berlin_oak_summary <- tibble::tibble(
  metric = c("Berlin oak observations", "Berlin recorded oak species", "Share of Berlin observations that are oak"),
  value = c(
    format_number(nrow(berlin_oaks)),
    format_number(n_distinct(berlin_oaks$level3_species)),
    ifelse(nrow(berlin) > 0, format_percent(nrow(berlin_oaks) / nrow(berlin)), "0%")
  )
)
nice_table(berlin_oak_summary, "Berlin oak observation summary")
```

```{r berlin-oak-local-areas}
if ("district" %in% names(berlin_oaks) && any(!is.na(berlin_oaks$district))) {
  berlin_oak_area_counts <- berlin_oaks |>
    filter(!is.na(district), district != "") |>
    count(district, name = "oak_observations", sort = TRUE)
} else {
  berlin_oak_area_counts <- tibble::tibble()
}

if (nrow(berlin_oak_area_counts) > 0) {
  berlin_oak_area_counts |>
    slice_head(n = 20) |>
    mutate(oak_observations = format_number(oak_observations)) |>
    nice_table("Top Berlin local areas by recorded oak observations")
}
```

```{r berlin-oak-map, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
berlin_oak_points_for_map <- sample_up_to(berlin_oaks, max_berlin_points)

if (nrow(berlin_oak_points_for_map) == 0) {
  empty_plot("No Berlin oak observations were available for the oak map.")
} else if (has_berlin_districts) {
  p <- ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = berlin_districts, fill = "gray98", color = "gray75", linewidth = 0.25)
  if (nrow(berlin_oak_points_for_map) >= 3) {
    p <- p +
      stat_density_2d_filled(data = berlin_oak_points_for_map,
                             aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, fill = after_stat(level)),
                             contour_var = "ndensity", bins = 7, alpha = 0.72)
  }
  p +
    geom_point(data = berlin_oak_points_for_map, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude),
               color = "#4d2c0b", alpha = 0.45, size = 0.75) +
    geom_sf(data = berlin_districts, fill = NA, color = "gray25", linewidth = 0.35) +
    coord_sf() +
    scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "B", direction = -1, name = "Oak density") +
    labs(title = "Recorded oak tree groups in Berlin",
         subtitle = "Oak observations are filtered from Quercus records and mapped with local-area boundaries.",
         caption = paste("Displayed oak points:", format_number(nrow(berlin_oak_points_for_map)), "of", format_number(nrow(berlin_oaks)), "Berlin oak observations."),
         x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_map_gtree()
} else {
  ggplot(berlin_oak_points_for_map, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude)) +
    geom_point(color = "#4d2c0b", alpha = 0.45, size = 0.75) +
    coord_fixed() +
    labs(title = "Recorded oak tree groups in Berlin",
         subtitle = "District borders were unavailable, so this map uses the Berlin bounding-box fallback.",
         x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") +
    theme_gtree()
}
```

```{r berlin-oak-area-bar, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=6}
if (nrow(berlin_oak_area_counts) == 0) {
  empty_plot("Berlin oak local-area counts are unavailable.")
} else {
  berlin_oak_area_counts |>
    slice_head(n = 20) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = reorder(district, oak_observations), y = oak_observations)) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    geom_text(aes(label = format_number(oak_observations)), hjust = -0.05, size = 3) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
    labs(title = "Recorded oak observations by Berlin local area",
         subtitle = "This helps locate oak record groups that may need monitoring for oak processionary risk.",
         x = NULL, y = "Oak observations") +
    theme_gtree()
}
```

**Interpretation.** The oak map and local-area ranking show where recorded oak groups are concentrated across Berlin. High-density areas in the dataset are candidates for targeted monitoring and public warning campaigns, though the records reflect observer activity and are not a complete oak census. This analysis demonstrates how the GlobalGeoTree dataset can be used for practical applications beyond general biodiversity research.

# Baden-Württemberg

Baden-Württemberg is a large state in southwestern Germany. It includes the Black Forest, the Rhine valley, and the Stuttgart metropolitan area. Its landscape diversity — from lowland river valleys to forested mountain ranges — makes it an interesting contrast to the uniformly urban Berlin.

## Load Baden-Württemberg boundaries

```{r load-bw-boundaries}
bw_boundary <- get_bundesland_boundary(bundeslaender, "baden|württemberg|wuerttemberg|wurttemberg")
bw_districts <- prepare_nuts3_districts(nuts3, nuts_prefix = "DE1", fallback_label = "Baden-Württemberg district")

has_bw_boundary <- !is.null(bw_boundary) && nrow(bw_boundary) > 0
has_bw_districts <- !is.null(bw_districts) && nrow(bw_districts) > 0

bw_boundary_status <- tibble::tibble(
  item = c("Baden-Württemberg boundary available", "NUTS3 boundary status", "Baden-Württemberg district polygons"),
  value = c(ifelse(has_bw_boundary, "Yes", "No"), nuts3_result$note, ifelse(has_bw_districts, format_number(nrow(bw_districts)), "0"))
)
nice_table(bw_boundary_status, "Baden-Württemberg boundary check")
```

## Filter observations to Baden-Württemberg

```{r filter-bw}
bw_filtered <- filter_state_observations(
  points_sf = germany_points, fallback_data = germany,
  boundary_data = bw_boundary, fallback_bbox = bw_bbox,
  boundary_note = "Spatial join to official NUTS1 Baden-Württemberg boundary",
  fallback_note = "Approximate Baden-Württemberg bounding box fallback"
)
bw <- bw_filtered$data
bw_summary <- make_state_summary(bw, "Baden-Württemberg", bw_filtered$note)
nice_table(bw_summary, "Baden-Württemberg observation summary")
```

## Baden-Württemberg observation sources

```{r bw-source-summary}
bw_source_counts <- make_source_counts(bw)
if (nrow(bw_source_counts) == 0) {
  nice_table(tibble::tibble(note = "No Baden-Württemberg source records were available."))
} else {
  bw_source_counts |>
    mutate(observations = format_number(observations), share = format_percent(share)) |>
    nice_table("Baden-Württemberg observations by source")
}
```

```{r bw-source-bar, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=5}
if (nrow(bw_source_counts) == 0) {
  empty_plot("No Baden-Württemberg source records were available.")
} else {
  ggplot(bw_source_counts, aes(x = source_short, y = observations)) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.05, size = 3) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
    labs(title = "Baden-Württemberg observations by source", x = NULL, y = "Observations") +
    theme_gtree()
}
```

## Baden-Württemberg observation density maps

This section addresses **RQ4.5** for Baden-Württemberg. As with the Germany-wide maps, three density styles are shown to provide complementary views of the spatial distribution.

```{r bw-density-main, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
bw_points_for_map <- sample_up_to(bw, max_bw_points)
bw_boundary_for_map <- if (has_bw_boundary) bw_boundary else NULL

if (nrow(bw_points_for_map) < 3) {
  empty_plot("Not enough Baden-Württemberg observations were available for the density map.")
} else {
  plot_filled_density_map(
    points_data = bw_points_for_map, boundary_data = bw_boundary_for_map,
    title = "Baden-Württemberg observations: smooth filled density",
    subtitle = "A clean hotspot view for comparing broader concentration areas.",
    caption = "This shows recording density in the dataset, not true tree abundance.",
    bins = 9, alpha = 0.90
  )
}
```

**Interpretation.** The filled density map highlights where recording activity is concentrated within Baden-Württemberg. Hotspots are likely to correspond to major urban areas and well-known natural areas rather than reflecting uniform tree distribution across the state.

### Alternative view: raw observation points

```{r bw-density-points, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
if (nrow(bw_points_for_map) < 1) {
  empty_plot("No Baden-Württemberg observations were available for the point map.")
} else {
  plot_points_only_map(
    points_data = bw_points_for_map, boundary_data = bw_boundary_for_map,
    title = "Baden-Württemberg observations: sampled points",
    subtitle = "Raw-point reference map with no smoothing.",
    caption = paste("Displayed points:", format_number(nrow(bw_points_for_map)), "of", format_number(nrow(bw)), "Baden-Württemberg observations."),
    point_alpha = 0.16, point_size = 0.55
  )
}
```

### Alternative view: points with density contours

```{r bw-density-contours, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
if (nrow(bw_points_for_map) < 3) {
  empty_plot("Not enough Baden-Württemberg observations were available for the contour map.")
} else {
  plot_points_contours_map(
    points_data = bw_points_for_map, boundary_data = bw_boundary_for_map,
    title = "Baden-Württemberg observations: density contours plus points",
    subtitle = "Contours show broad concentration zones while sampled points remain visible.",
    caption = paste("Displayed points:", format_number(nrow(bw_points_for_map)), "of", format_number(nrow(bw)), "Baden-Württemberg observations."),
    point_alpha = 0.16, point_size = 0.55, bins = 9
  )
}
```

## Baden-Württemberg districts: observations and species

```{r bw-district-join}
# Join observations to NUTS3 district polygons and compute per-district statistics
bw_district_outputs <- make_district_outputs(bw, bw_districts)
bw_district_counts <- bw_district_outputs$counts
bw_district_map <- bw_district_outputs$map

if (nrow(bw_district_counts) > 0) {
  bw_district_counts |>
    slice_head(n = 20) |>
    mutate(observations = format_number(observations), species = format_number(species), sources = format_number(sources)) |>
    nice_table("Top Baden-Württemberg NUTS3 districts by observation count")
} else {
  nice_table(tibble::tibble(note = "Baden-Württemberg district counts are unavailable because NUTS3 polygons were not loaded."))
}
```

```{r bw-district-bar, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=6}
if (nrow(bw_district_counts) == 0) {
  empty_plot("Baden-Württemberg district counts are unavailable because NUTS3 polygons were not loaded.")
} else {
  bw_district_counts |>
    slice_head(n = 20) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = reorder(district_name, observations), y = observations)) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    geom_text(aes(label = format_number(observations)), hjust = -0.05, size = 3) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
    labs(title = "Baden-Württemberg observations by NUTS3 district", subtitle = "Only the top 20 districts are shown.", x = NULL, y = "Observations") +
    theme_gtree()
}
```

```{r bw-district-species-bar, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=6}
if (nrow(bw_district_counts) == 0) {
  empty_plot("Baden-Württemberg district species counts are unavailable.")
} else {
  bw_district_counts |>
    arrange(desc(species)) |>
    slice_head(n = 20) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = reorder(district_name, species), y = species)) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    geom_text(aes(label = format_number(species)), hjust = -0.05, size = 3) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
    labs(title = "Recorded species by Baden-Württemberg NUTS3 district", x = NULL, y = "Recorded species") +
    theme_gtree()
}
```

```{r bw-district-map, fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
if (is.null(bw_district_map)) {
  empty_plot("Baden-Württemberg district map is unavailable because NUTS3 polygons were not loaded.")
} else {
  ggplot(bw_district_map) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = observations), color = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", trans = "sqrt", labels = scales::comma_format()) +
    labs(title = "Observation frequency across Baden-Württemberg NUTS3 districts",
         subtitle = "Square-root scaling improves readability when a few districts have very high counts.",
         fill = "Observations") +
    theme_map_gtree()
}
```

**Interpretation.** The district-level view reveals which parts of Baden-Württemberg are most actively recorded. Urban districts with large populations tend to have more observations, likely because citizen-science platforms have more users there.

## Sources on the Baden-Württemberg map

```{r bw-source-map, fig.width=9, fig.height=7}
bw_top_source_names <- bw |> count(source_raw, sort = TRUE) |> slice_head(n = 4) |> pull(source_raw)

bw_source_points <- bw |>
  filter(source_raw %in% bw_top_source_names) |>
  mutate(source_display = make_source_label(source_raw)) |>
  group_by(source_display) |>
  group_modify(~ sample_up_to(.x, as.integer(max_bw_points / 4))) |>
  ungroup()

if (nrow(bw_source_points) == 0) {
  empty_plot("No source-specific Baden-Württemberg points were available for mapping.")
} else {
  p <- ggplot()
  if (has_bw_boundary) {
    p <- p + geom_sf(data = bw_boundary, fill = "gray97", color = "gray60", linewidth = 0.35)
  }
  p +
    geom_point(data = bw_source_points, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, color = source_display), alpha = 0.24, size = 0.45) +
    facet_wrap(~ source_display, ncol = 2) +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2", guide = "none") +
    coord_sf() +
    labs(title = "Spatial patterns of the largest Baden-Württemberg observation sources",
         subtitle = "Facets show the four largest source groups. Points are sampled for readability.",
         x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_map_gtree(base_size = 11)
}
```

**Interpretation.** If different source panels show different spatial patterns, the overall density map for Baden-Württemberg reflects a combination of ecological signal and platform-specific coverage. Sources concentrated in urban areas contribute different patterns than those focused on rural or forested regions.

## Top recorded species in Baden-Württemberg

```{r bw-top-species}
bw_named <- add_species_display_name(bw)

bw_top_species <- bw_named |>
  count(level3_species, species_display_name, display_common_name_en, sort = TRUE, name = "observations") |>
  mutate(share = observations / sum(observations))

bw_top_species |>
  slice_head(n = 20) |>
  select(scientific_name = level3_species, common_name_en = display_common_name_en, observations, share) |>
  mutate(observations = format_number(observations), share = format_percent(share)) |>
  nice_table("Top recorded species in Baden-Württemberg")
```

```{r bw-top-species-bar, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=6}
bw_top_species |>
  slice_head(n = 15) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(species_display_name, observations), y = observations)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = format_number(observations)), hjust = -0.05, size = 3) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(title = "Most recorded tree species in Baden-Württemberg",
       subtitle = "Common names are shown where available; counts refer to GlobalGeoTree observations.",
       x = NULL, y = "Observations") +
  theme_gtree()
```

**Interpretation.** The most recorded species in Baden-Württemberg likely include both common native forest trees and widely planted urban species. Comparing this list with Berlin's reveals whether the same species dominate across regions or whether each region has a distinctive species profile — a question examined directly in the Regional Comparison section below.

# Nordrhein-Westfalen (NRW)

Nordrhein-Westfalen is Germany's most populous state, containing the Ruhr metropolitan area and several major cities including Cologne, Düsseldorf, Dortmund, and Essen. Its high population density may correlate with high citizen-science recording activity, making it a particularly interesting case for understanding the relationship between population and observation density.

## Load NRW boundaries

```{r load-nrw-boundaries}
nrw_boundary <- get_bundesland_boundary(bundeslaender, "nordrhein|north rhine|westfalen|westphalia")
nrw_districts <- prepare_nuts3_districts(nuts3, nuts_prefix = "DEA", fallback_label = "NRW district")

has_nrw_boundary <- !is.null(nrw_boundary) && nrow(nrw_boundary) > 0
has_nrw_districts <- !is.null(nrw_districts) && nrow(nrw_districts) > 0

nrw_boundary_status <- tibble::tibble(
  item = c("NRW boundary available", "NUTS3 boundary status", "NRW district polygons"),
  value = c(ifelse(has_nrw_boundary, "Yes", "No"), nuts3_result$note, ifelse(has_nrw_districts, format_number(nrow(nrw_districts)), "0"))
)
nice_table(nrw_boundary_status, "NRW boundary check")
```

nrw_filtered <- filter_state_observations(
  points_sf = germany_points, fallback_data = germany,
  boundary_data = nrw_boundary, fallback_bbox = nrw_bbox,
  boundary_note = "Spatial join to official NUTS1 NRW boundary",
  fallback_note = "Approximate NRW bounding box fallback"

# Regional Comparison: Berlin, Baden-Württemberg and NRW

This section addresses **RQ4.6 and RQ4.7** directly. The three regions were examined separately in the sections above; placing them side by side makes it easier to see whether they differ in record volume, species richness, dominant species, and source composition. The summary table below provides a concise overview of all three regions.

```{r regional-comparison-data}
# Define the region order for consistent display across all comparison charts
region_levels <- c("Berlin", "Baden-Württemberg", "NRW")

# Combine observations from all three regions into one data frame
region_records <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  berlin_named |> mutate(region = "Berlin"),
  bw_named |> mutate(region = "Baden-Württemberg"),
  nrw_named |> mutate(region = "NRW")
) |>
  mutate(region = factor(region, levels = region_levels))

# Compute summary metrics for each region
regional_summary <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  make_region_metrics(berlin_named, "Berlin"),
  make_region_metrics(bw_named, "Baden-Württemberg"),
  make_region_metrics(nrw_named, "NRW")
) |>
  mutate(
    region = factor(region, levels = region_levels),
    observations_per_species = ifelse(recorded_species > 0, observations / recorded_species, NA_real_)
  )

regional_summary |>
  mutate(
    observations = format_number(observations),
    recorded_species = format_number(recorded_species),
    recorded_genera = format_number(recorded_genera),
    recorded_families = format_number(recorded_families),
    data_sources = format_number(data_sources),
    observations_per_species = scales::number(observations_per_species, accuracy = 0.1)
  ) |>
  nice_table("Regional comparison summary")
```

```{r regional-observation-bar, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=4.8}
ggplot(regional_summary, aes(x = region, y = observations)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = format_number(observations)), vjust = -0.35, size = 3.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.14))) +
  labs(title = "Observation records by region",
       subtitle = "Counts compare GlobalGeoTree records, not true tree abundance.",
       x = NULL, y = "Observations") +
  theme_gtree()
```

```{r regional-species-bar, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=4.8}
ggplot(regional_summary, aes(x = region, y = recorded_species)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = format_number(recorded_species)), vjust = -0.35, size = 3.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma_format(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.14))) +
  labs(title = "Recorded species by region",
       subtitle = "This counts distinct Latin species names recorded in each regional subset.",
       x = NULL, y = "Recorded species") +
  theme_gtree()
```

**Interpretation.** Comparing observations and species counts together helps separate recording volume from taxonomic coverage. A region with many records but relatively few species may be heavily observed with a narrow focus; a region with fewer records but many species may reflect a more diverse recording effort.

## Regional top species overlap

This heatmap answers **RQ4.6** across all three regions at once: are the same species dominant everywhere, or does each region have a distinctive species composition?

```{r regional-top-species-overlap, fig.width=9.5, fig.height=7}
regional_species_counts <- region_records |>
  filter(!is.na(level3_species), level3_species != "") |>
  count(region, level3_species, species_display_name, name = "observations") |>
  group_by(region) |>
  mutate(region_observations = sum(observations), regional_share = observations / region_observations) |>
  ungroup()

regional_top_species <- regional_species_counts |>
  group_by(level3_species, species_display_name) |>
  summarise(total_observations = sum(observations), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(total_observations)) |>
  slice_head(n = 18)

if (nrow(regional_top_species) == 0) {
  empty_plot("No regional species records were available for the comparison heatmap.")
} else {
  regional_species_heatmap <- expand.grid(
    region = region_levels, level3_species = regional_top_species$level3_species, stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ) |>
    tibble::as_tibble() |>
    left_join(regional_top_species |> select(level3_species, species_display_name, total_observations), by = "level3_species") |>
    left_join(regional_species_counts |> select(region, level3_species, observations, regional_share), by = c("region", "level3_species")) |>
    mutate(
      observations = dplyr::coalesce(observations, 0L),
      regional_share = dplyr::coalesce(regional_share, 0),
      region = factor(region, levels = region_levels),
      species_display_name = factor(species_display_name, levels = rev(unique(regional_top_species$species_display_name))),
      count_label = ifelse(observations > 0, format_number(observations), "")
    )

  ggplot(regional_species_heatmap, aes(x = region, y = species_display_name, fill = regional_share)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.35) +
    geom_text(aes(label = count_label), size = 2.8) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 0.1), name = "Regional\nshare") +
    labs(title = "Top recorded tree species across Berlin, Baden-Württemberg and NRW",
         subtitle = "Fill shows each species' share within a region; labels show observation counts.",
         x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme_gtree(base_size = 11) +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9))
}
```

**Interpretation.** Species that appear dark across all three columns are consistently prominent regardless of region — these are likely widespread native or commonly planted trees. A species that is dark in only one column may be genuinely more common there, or it may simply reflect the geographic focus of a dominant platform in that region. Species that appear in all three regions with similar shares suggest a shared ecological or urban-planting baseline.

## Regional source composition

This stacked bar chart completes the answer to **RQ4.7**. Differences in observation volume or top species between regions could reflect true ecological differences or simply different data platforms.

```{r regional-source-composition, fig.width=8.5, fig.height=5.5}
regional_source_counts <- region_records |>
  mutate(source_display = make_source_label(source_raw)) |>
  count(region, source_display, name = "observations")

top_regional_source_groups <- regional_source_counts |>
  group_by(source_display) |>
  summarise(total_observations = sum(observations), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(total_observations)) |>
  slice_head(n = 6) |>
  pull(source_display)

regional_source_levels <- unique(c(setdiff(top_regional_source_groups, "Other sources"), "Other sources"))

regional_source_comparison <- regional_source_counts |>
  mutate(source_display = if_else(source_display %in% top_regional_source_groups, source_display, "Other sources")) |>
  group_by(region, source_display) |>
  summarise(observations = sum(observations), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(region) |>
  mutate(share = observations / sum(observations)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(region = factor(region, levels = region_levels),
         source_display = factor(source_display, levels = regional_source_levels))

if (nrow(regional_source_comparison) == 0) {
  empty_plot("No regional source records were available for comparison.")
} else {
  ggplot(regional_source_comparison, aes(x = region, y = share, fill = source_display)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.72) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
    labs(title = "Source composition by region",
         subtitle = "Each bar sums to 100%; source groups are shortened for readability.",
         x = NULL, y = "Share of regional observations", fill = "Source group") +
    theme_gtree()
}
```

**Interpretation.** If regions share a similar source composition, regional differences in density and species rankings are more likely to be ecologically meaningful. If one region is dominated by a different platform, any apparent regional difference must be interpreted with caution.

# Overall Interpretation

This report has addressed three groups of research questions about the GlobalGeoTree dataset. The findings are summarised below.

**RQ2 — Source and Platform Bias.** The dataset is highly concentrated: citizen-science platforms — above all iNaturalist — provide the vast majority of records (RQ2.1, RQ2.2). Source composition varies systematically by country, with some countries covered almost entirely by a single platform and others showing a more balanced mix (RQ2.3). Different source groups also record different plant families at different rates, indicating taxonomic bias alongside geographic bias (RQ2.4). The source-specific world maps confirm that each major platform leaves a distinct spatial footprint, meaning the combined dataset is a composite of several geographically non-uniform "lenses" rather than a single coherent survey.

**RQ3 — Temporal Development.** The overall number of observations rose substantially between `r start_year` and `r end_year` (RQ3.1), with the strongest growth concentrated in specific years (RQ3.2). However, this growth is largely driven by the expansion of iNaturalist and other citizen-science platforms rather than by a broad increase across all source types (RQ3.4). Geographic coverage did genuinely expand over the study period, with new countries and grid cells entering the dataset over time, but that expansion is uneven and concentrated in regions where the dominant platforms have an active user base (RQ3.3). The apparent decline in `r end_year` is most likely a data-export artifact.

**RQ4 — Germany Regional Analysis.** Within Germany, the national density map is shaped by several platforms with partially different spatial footprints (RQ4.1, RQ4.3). Recording activity has grown strongly in recent years, following the same citizen-science trend visible globally (RQ4.2). At the Bundesland level, observation counts vary widely, reflecting differences in population density, platform coverage, and observer activity (RQ4.4). The three focal regions — Berlin, Baden-Württemberg, and NRW — differ in observation volume, species richness, and source composition (RQ4.5, RQ4.6, RQ4.7). These differences must be interpreted alongside the source structure rather than treated as purely ecological. The Berlin oak analysis (RQ4.8) demonstrates a practical application of the dataset: identifying areas with high concentrations of recorded oak trees to support monitoring of oak processionary moth risk.

**Limitations and outlook.** All visualisations in this report show **recording intensity** in the dataset, not a direct census of trees. High values can reflect true tree presence, but they equally reflect where observers and platforms are most active. For any analysis built on GlobalGeoTree, the source composition of the sample should be reported alongside geographic, temporal, or taxonomic results, and key findings should be checked with and without the largest citizen-science source. Future work could refine the source classification rules, particularly for non-English source names, and explore whether the patterns observed in this analysis hold when the dominant citizen-science sources are excluded as a sensitivity check.
